prompt.context: Our client is a major media conglomerate with radio stations, magazines, and newspapers throughout the US. They have five major newspapers in five important metropolitan areas. Its oldest newspaper circulates in the Seattle metropolitan area. After 50 years of great profitability and steady market, early this year there was a strong decrease in market share and price.
prompt.question: The CEO has hired A.T. Kearney to help understand the new market dynamics and determine what strategy should be taken next. The CEO is also expecting us to provide advice on whether he should increase prices. How would you go about addressing this question?

clarifying_info.q: How was the market structured before the change?
clarifying_info.a: For over 50 years the Seattle newspaper split the market 50-50 with a strong but independent local newspaper. Both are well recognized for their news quality.

clarifying_info.q: What happened to the competitive landscape?
clarifying_info.a: Earlier this year a new newspaper entered the market, capturing 50% market share in less than nine months and leaving the two former newspapers with 25% each. The new entrant is recognized for offering lower quality news than the two established players.

clarifying_info.q: What did our client do in response to the new entrant?
clarifying_info.a: Our client dropped its price to match the new entrant's price of $0.50. The old competitor followed. This has not been enough to recapture the loss in market share.

clarifying_info.q: Do any of the newspapers offer subscriptions?
clarifying_info.a: No. None of the players offer subscriptions.

clarifying_info.q: Do any of the newspapers have online news?
clarifying_info.a: No. None of the players have online news.

clarifying_info.q: Are there fixed costs to operating a newspaper?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there are high fixed costs, but they are considered sunk costs.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a cartel or pricing arrangement for distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. There is a cartel for distribution, which sets delivery cost at 40% of price for all players.

exhibits.title: Market Data Before and After New Entrant
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of key metrics for the client, old competitor, and new competitor before and after the new entrant arrived

exhibits.title: Cost Structure Before and After New Entrant
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of cost-related metrics for all players before and after

exhibits.title: Daily Advertising Revenue Before and After New Entrant
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of daily advertising revenue for all players before and after

framework: Understand market demand: overall market size, growth trends, and customer segments in Seattle
Analyze competitive landscape: market share changes, pricing, product quality, and new entrant's strategy
Assess revenue streams: newspaper sales revenue and advertising revenue (pre- and post-entry)
Analyze cost structure: per-unit variable costs (production + delivery) versus price, and fixed costs
Determine profitability impact: calculate profit per paper before and after, net of all revenues
Evaluate pricing strategy: assess whether raising price back toward $1 is viable given competitive dynamics
Identify strategic options: respond to new market niche created by the low-quality entrant

questions.prompt: How has market share and volume changed with the new entrant, and what does this tell you about the competitive situation?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates note that the total market grew: before = 4,000 units/day; after = 10,000 units/day. The client's volume actually increased from 2,000 to 2,500 despite losing market share (50% to 25%). This implies the new entrant created a new market segment (lower-income or lower-quality-seeking readers) rather than purely cannibalizing existing readers. The new competitor targets a different niche — lower quality news at a lower price — and is not a direct competitor in the quality segment.

questions.prompt: Calculate the client's daily newspaper sales revenue before and after the new entrant. What is the revenue impact?
questions.guidance: Before: $1.00 x 2,000 = $2,000/day. After: $0.50 x 2,500 = $1,250/day. This is a 37.5% decline in newspaper sales revenue despite volume increase. Key insight: the price drop more than offset the volume gain.

math.setup: Revenue = Price x Daily Sales Volume

questions.prompt: Calculate the client's cost per newspaper before and after the new entrant. Is the client making money on each paper sold?
questions.guidance: Variable cost per paper = production cost + delivery cost. Production cost = pages/day x cost/page = 40 x $0.01 = $0.40. Delivery cost = 40% of price = 40% x $0.50 = $0.20. Total variable cost = $0.60/paper. This exceeds the $0.50 sales price by $0.10. Contrast with the new competitor: 20 pages x $0.01 = $0.20 production + $0.20 delivery = $0.40/paper cost vs. $0.50 price, giving a $0.10 margin. The client is loss-making on per-paper sales at the current price; its fixed costs are sunk.

math.setup: Variable cost per paper = (Pages/day x Cost/page) + (Delivery Cost % x Price)
steps: New competitor production cost: 20 pages x $0.01 = $0.20/paper
math.answer: Client loses $0.10 per paper sold at $0.50 price; new competitor earns $0.10 margin per paper

questions.prompt: The interviewer says the client is still making a profit despite losing money on paper sales. How is this possible?
questions.guidance: The client earns $2,000/day in advertising revenue, unchanged from before the new entrant. This advertising revenue more than offsets the per-paper loss. Daily net contribution after variable costs: Sales revenue ($1,250) - Variable costs (2,500 x $0.60 = $1,500) + Advertising ($2,000) = $1,750/day profit contribution. Key insight: advertising revenue subsidizes and more than covers the shortfall from newspaper sales at $0.50. The new competitor has $0 in advertising revenue, suggesting it serves a market segment that is not attractive to advertisers — confirming it has created a new, separate market niche.

math.setup: Daily profit contribution = Sales revenue - Variable costs + Advertising revenue
math.answer: Client earns $1,750/day profit contribution; advertising revenue of $2,000/day more than offsets the $250/day loss on paper sales

questions.prompt: Why does the new competitor have $0 in advertising revenue, even though it has 5,000 daily readers — more than either established player?
questions.guidance: Companies allocate advertising budgets across channels that reach their target customers. The new competitor's lower-quality, lower-income reader base is not the target demographic for existing advertisers who had been placing ads in the quality newspapers. Advertisers have not shifted budget to the new entrant. This confirms that the new competitor has created a distinct market segment with different demographics — it is not taking the client's readers or advertiser relationships.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options should the CEO consider going forward?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Raise price back to $1.00 — the new competitor is not a direct quality competitor; established quality readers will likely remain
At $1.00 price the client's variable cost ($0.40 production + $0.40 delivery) = $0.80/paper, giving a $0.20/paper margin plus $2,000 advertising — significantly better economics
$0.50 is unsustainable long-run for the client given its higher production cost (40 pages) versus the new entrant (20 pages)

categories.name: New market segment entry
ideas: Launch a separate, lower-quality newspaper targeting the new price-sensitive niche created by the new entrant
Leverage existing printing infrastructure; in worst case earn $0.10 margin/paper x 5,000 papers = $500/day from printing
A separate brand keeps quality positioning of the flagship paper intact
Could attract new advertisers targeting the lower-income demographic

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Explore reducing pages or page costs to improve per-paper economics at $0.50 if price increase is not feasible
Renegotiate delivery cartel terms if possible

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Explore increasing advertising rates given higher total market readership
Consider online/digital presence to open new revenue streams
Introduce subscription model to stabilize revenue base

recommendation: Raise the cover price back toward $1.00. The new entrant targets a distinct, lower-quality market segment and is not a direct competitor for quality-conscious readers. Price matching was not necessary and has significantly damaged economics.
Explore launching a separate low-cost, lower-quality newspaper (or acquiring the new entrant) to capture the newly created market segment without cannibalizing the flagship brand.
risks: Raising price may cause some price-sensitive readers to defect to the new entrant, reducing volume below 2,500
If advertisers value circulation numbers, a volume decline could affect advertising revenue
A new low-cost product could cannibalize the flagship if not kept as a distinct brand
The delivery cartel constrains cost flexibility — delivery costs will rise proportionally with any price increase
next_steps: Conduct reader segmentation analysis to quantify how many current readers are price-sensitive vs. quality-loyal
Model advertising revenue sensitivity to circulation changes before finalizing price increase
Develop business case for a new low-cost newspaper product targeting the new market niche
Monitor whether the new entrant gains advertising revenue over time as an indicator of market maturity
